title: Edamame vs. chickpeas: protein, fiber, and calories

seo.title: Edamame vs. chickpeas: protein, fiber, and calories
seo.meta_description: Edamame is higher in protein and lower in carbs; chickpeas usually provide more fiber. Compare both cooked per 100 g and per serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked edamame and chickpeas for protein, fiber, calories, carbohydrate, fat, and protein quality.

excerpt: Cooked edamame is usually higher in protein and lower in carbohydrate than chickpeas: about 12 grams of protein and 121 calories per 100 grams versus roughly 9 grams and 164 calories. Chickpeas generally provide more fiber—around 7–8 grams versus about 5—and much more starch. They are not two versions of the same legume but distinct nutrition profiles.
content_html:
Edamame and chickpeas are both legumes, but they divide their macronutrients quite differently. Edamame is soybean harvested while still green and carries more protein and fat; chickpeas are mature seeds that store much more starch and usually more fiber as well.

Edamame is more efficient when protein per calorie is the priority. Chickpeas bring more fiber and more complex carbohydrate, which can be exactly what a meal needs when energy matters too.

Per 100 grams cooked, the differences are clear

Per 100 g cookedEdamameChickpeas
Protein~12 g~8.9 g
Calories~121~164
Carbohydrate~9 g~27 g
Fiber~5 g~7.6 g
Fat~5 g~2.6 g

Edamame provides about 3 extra grams of protein and roughly 43 fewer calories per 100 grams. The biggest split is carbohydrate: chickpeas contain about three times as much because the mature seed stores far more starch.

A real serving puts the protein difference in context

About 150 grams of edamame provide roughly 18 grams of protein and 182 calories. The same amount of chickpeas provides around 13 grams of protein and 246 calories.

Both can make a meaningful contribution to a protein-rich meal. Edamame simply reaches a higher protein amount with less total energy, while chickpeas also supply substantially more carbohydrate.

Chickpeas have a clear fiber advantage

A 150-gram serving can provide roughly 11–12 grams of fiber from chickpeas versus about 7–8 grams from edamame. Both are strong sources, but this is a meaningful difference.

And those 27 grams of carbohydrate per 100 grams do not mean chickpeas are “sugary.” Much of that carbohydrate is starch and fiber rather than simple sugars.

Edamame contains more fat, mostly unsaturated

Edamame provides about 5 grams of fat per 100 grams, roughly twice as much as chickpeas. Most of it reflects soybeans' naturally unsaturated fat profile.

That helps explain why edamame is not dramatically lower in calories despite having far fewer carbs: some of its energy comes from fat instead.

Soy protein has an especially complete amino acid profile

Soy contains all nine essential amino acids in favorable proportions. Chickpeas contain all essential amino acids too, although some, including methionine, are present in lower proportions.

That does not mean chickpeas must be eaten with rice at the same meal. A varied diet across the day readily complements amino acids from different plant foods.

Both contribute useful micronutrients

Edamame and chickpeas provide folate, iron, magnesium and potassium. The iron in both is nonheme and can be absorbed more effectively when the meal also includes a vitamin-C-rich food such as peppers, tomatoes, citrus or fruit.

Which should you choose?

If you want more protein with fewer calories and fewer carbs, edamame has the advantage. If you want more fiber and a starchier legume that still provides useful protein, chickpeas fit better.

They are not perfect rivals or exact substitutes: they are two legumes with different balances of protein, fiber, fat and starch, which is why they work well in different meals.

faq.question: Which has more protein, edamame or chickpeas?
faq.answer: Cooked edamame provides about 12 g protein per 100 g versus roughly 8.9 g in cooked chickpeas.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Chickpeas usually do: about 7.6 g fiber per 100 g cooked versus roughly 5 g in edamame.

faq.question: Is edamame a complete protein?
faq.answer: Yes. As a soy food, edamame contains all nine essential amino acids in a high-quality plant-protein profile.
